topics: 📖 Megillah and Zimun — women are included because 'they too were part of that miracle'; a minor who knows to Whom he blesses joins a zimun
🩹 A Minor's Impurity — how 'nefashot' and 'adam' fold a day-old infant into the impurities of ziva, tzara'at, and a corpse
🐄 Parah Adumah — sanctifying the ashes (minor vs. woman) and the validity of an uncircumcised man's sprinkling
🔪 Slaughter and Aliyah — a Samaritan's and an apostate's slaughter; compelling even a slave to move to Eretz Yisrael or Jerusalem
⛺ Are Priests 'Obviously' Obligated? — sukka, tzitzit, tefillin, and shofar all needed to specify priests explicitly
🎺 Tefillin of the Head vs. the Arm — why exemption from one does not exempt a priest from the other

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The 'Everyone' Sugya Continues
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 3a–3b
overview.hebrewSource: הַכֹּל חַיָּיבִין בְּסוּכָּה, כֹּהֲנִים לְוִיִּם וְיִשְׂרְאֵלִים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara keeps mining every mishnaic 'everyone' (hakol) for its hidden addition. It works through megilla reading and zimun (adding women, slaves, and a minor who knows to Whom he blesses); the impurities of ziva, tzara'at, and a corpse, each folding in a day-old infant via an extra word in its verse; who may sanctify the Parah Adumah ashes or sprinkle its water; who may slaughter; and who can be compelled to move to Eretz Yisrael or Jerusalem. The sugya then turns to a repeated question — why is it not obvious that priests, Levites, and Israelites are obligated in sukka, tzitzit, tefillin, and shofar? — and shows how each mitzva's own verse could have exempted priests specifically, so the baraita must state their inclusion explicitly.

slides.title: 📖 Megillah and Zimun — Who Else Is Included
slides.subtitle: Two more 'everyone' clauses, two more hidden additions
rows: Everyone is obligated in reading the Megilla
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: 'they too were participants in that miracle'
Women and slaves — each forms its own zimun
Baraita: 'women recite zimun for themselves, slaves for themselves'
A minor who knows to Whom one recites a blessing

slides.title: 🩹 Does a Minor Become Impure? The Verse's Hidden Yes
slides.subtitle: Tzara'at (leprous marks) as the test case

nodes.content: ❓ 'Everyone becomes impure with leprous marks' (נגעים) — what does this add?
💭 Might think: the verse says אִישׁ צָרוּעַ — a leprous MAN — so an adult, yes; a minor, no

columns.label: But the verse also says
columns.content: אָדָם כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעוֹר בְּשָׂרוֹ — 'a person,' including everyone regardless of age

columns.label: So what does 'ish' teach?
columns.content: That a MALE leper tears his garments and lets his hair grow wild — a woman does not

nodes.content: ✅ A minor does become impure through tzara'at; 'ish' teaches a separate halakha about mourning practices

callout.label: Same technique for ziva and corpse impurity:
callout.text: A day-old infant with a zav-like discharge becomes impure (Rabbi Yehuda, from the doubled 'ish ish'); one who contracts corpse impurity is impure at any age, from 'the persons that were there' (Numbers 19:18) — though a minor is excluded from the karet penalty tied to the word 'ish'.

slides.title: 🐄 Parah Adumah and Slaughter: Three More 'Everyone' Clauses
slides.subtitle: Each broad statement hides a different, specific addition

boxes.title: Sanctifying the Ashes
items: Mishna: everyone is fit except a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor
Rabbi Yehuda: a minor IS fit
The Rabbis instead deem a woman fit (and a minor unfit)

boxes.title: Sprinkling the Water
items: 'Everyone is fit to sprinkle' adds one who is uncircumcised (עָרֵל)
Rabbi Elazar: an uncircumcised man's sprinkling is valid

boxes.title: Slaughtering
items: 'Everyone slaughters' adds a Samaritan (Kuti) — his slaughter is valid
And also adds an apostate Jew (Yisrael mumar)

callout.label: Also from 'everyone':
callout.text: One may compel his household to move even a slave to Eretz Yisrael or Jerusalem (or from a pleasant home to a poor one there), but none may be compelled to leave — not even from a poor home in Jerusalem to a pleasant one elsewhere.

slides.title: ⛺ Are Priests Really 'Obviously' Obligated?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara keeps asking why a baraita bothers to mention priests, Levites, and Israelites by name

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: 'Everyone is obligated in sukka, including priests, Levites, and Israelites' — isn't that obvious?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Not obvious: sukka is compared to one's home, where a man dwells with his wife. Priests, occupied with Temple service, might have been exempt entirely!

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: So how are they included after all?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: They are exempt only during their actual service — off-duty they are obligated, just like travelers, who are exempt from sukka by day but obligated at night.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Same question for tzitzit: priests wear diverse kinds (wool and linen) in their vestments during service — shouldn't that exempt them from tzitzit altogether?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Only during service is diverse kinds permitted to them; off-duty they may not wear it, so they remain obligated in tzitzit the rest of the time.

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Each mitzva's own verse could plausibly have carved priests out; the baraita has to say 'including priests' precisely because the exemption is a live possibility, not an obvious non-issue.

slides.title: 🎺 Tefillin of the Head, and Trumpets vs. Shofar
slides.subtitle: Two more cases where an apparent exemption for priests is dismantled

steps.content: 1️⃣ Priests cannot wear arm-tefillin during service — their vestments must touch the skin directly with nothing interposing. So perhaps they're also exempt from head-tefillin?
2️⃣ No: the two mitzvot don't depend on each other — 'absence of the arm-tefillin does not prevent the head-tefillin, and absence of the head-tefillin does not prevent the arm-tefillin'

3️⃣ Objection: doesn't the High Priest's mitre also interpose on the head, just like the vestments do on the arm? Answer: his hair was visible between the frontplate (tzitz) and the mitre — exactly where tefillin sit

4️⃣ Same logic for shofar: priests sound trumpets all year for the offerings, but trumpets and shofar are different mitzvot entirely — that doesn't exempt them from sounding the shofar on Rosh HaShana

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: An exemption from one mitzva never automatically bleeds into a similar-looking mitzva; each requires its own verse and its own proof.

summary.principle: The Gemara's clause-by-clause mining of 'everyone' (hakol) continues across megilla, zimun, the impurities of ziva/tzara'at/corpse, Parah Adumah, slaughter, and aliyah to the Land — and then flips to ask why priests specifically needed to be named as obligated in sukka, tzitzit, tefillin, and shofar, since their Temple service could plausibly have exempted them.

flowSteps.content: 📖 'Everyone' in megilla and zimun → adds women (megilla, per R' Yehoshua ben Levi), women and slaves (zimun), a minor who knows to Whom he blesses
🩹 'Everyone' in ziva/tzara'at/corpse impurity → each includes a day-old infant, derived from an extra word in its verse

columns.content: 🐄 Parah Adumah: R' Yehuda adds a minor; Rabbis add a woman instead; sprinkling adds an uncircumcised man
⛺ Priests need explicit inclusion in sukka/tzitzit/tefillin/shofar — exempt only during actual Temple service

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an exemption during Temple service is never automatic or total — it applies strictly to the hours of service, and never transfers to a similar mitzva without its own proof

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say women are obligated in reading the Megilla?
o: Because women are generally more scrupulous in performing mitzvot
Because they too were participants in that miracle
Because the verse mentions Esther by name
Because women are already obligated in Purim charity
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's stated reason is that women 'too were participants in that miracle' of Purim.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, how do women and slaves participate in zimun (the invitation to Grace after Meals)?
o: They may never form a zimun
They join a zimun only together with men
Women form a zimun for themselves, and slaves form a zimun for themselves
Only slaves may form a zimun, not women
quiz.e: The baraita states plainly: 'Women form a zimun for themselves and slaves form a zimun for themselves.'

quiz.q: How does the Gemara prove that even a minor becomes impure through tzara'at, despite the verse's phrase 'a leprous MAN'?
o: It doesn't — a minor is fully exempt
From 'אָדָם כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעוֹר בְּשָׂרוֹ' — 'a person,' which includes everyone regardless of age
From a comparison to the impurity of a corpse
From the fact that Miriam was afflicted with tzara'at
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that the verse 'when a person shall have in the skin of his flesh' includes all people, of any age, leaving 'ish' to teach a different, unrelated halakha.

quiz.q: Regarding who is added by 'everyone is fit to sanctify the ashes of the red heifer,' what is the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis?
o: Rabbi Yehuda deems a minor fit; the Rabbis instead deem a woman fit (and disqualify a minor)
Both agree a gentile is added
Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies women entirely while the Rabbis include them and a minor
There is no dispute — both include a minor
quiz.e: The mishna disqualifies a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor; Rabbi Yehuda deems a minor fit, while the Rabbis instead deem a woman fit and keep the minor disqualified.

quiz.q: Why are priests obligated in sukka only outside their hours of Temple service, according to the Gemara's resolution?
o: Because sukka is compared to dwelling at home with one's wife, and priests are exempt only while actually serving — like travelers, exempt by day but obligated at night
Because the Temple courtyard itself counts as their sukka
Because priests are entirely exempt from the mitzva of sukka
Because priests never marry during their years of service
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves that priests are exempt only during actual Temple service; off-duty they are obligated, drawing the same distinction made for travelers exempt from sukka by day but obligated at night.
